[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths and English, 'b = a' means b becomes an equal but independent copy, and 'a == b' means 'have the same values'. Java rule: for arrays, b = a copies only the reference, so both names denote one array, and == tests whether two names refer to the same array.
[1] misconception (M) -> ArrayEqualityComparesValues: wrong rule: a == b is true when a and b hold the same values. Right rule: == compares whether a and b are the same array (same reference), not whether their elements are equal.
[2] misconception (M) -> AssignmentCopiesObject: wrong rule: Assigning an array reference copies the array. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ArrayEqualityComparesValues: Points to LT: b = a copies the reference, so every later write through b is a write to the shared array. Inconsistent application: after b = a the trace changes b[0] but leaves a[0] unchanged in its table, keeping two copies on some steps and one array on others. (here mixing in: "a == b is true when a and b hold the same values")

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: aliasing is the situation in which two or more array variables refer to the same array object.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: an assignment makes the names a and b refer to the same array; an equality test a == b checks whether the two names refer to the same array.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: in b = a, a is evaluated to its reference value, which is then stored in b; no element is read or copied. In a == b both reference values are evaluated and compared.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: for int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; int[] b = {1, 2, 3};, the test a == b is false; after b = a it is true. A read through either name gives the same element.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: b = a changes only the variable b (it now holds a's reference). A later b[0] = 17 changes the one shared array, so a[0] then reads 17 too.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Only new creates a distinct array; to copy, create a new array and copy each element (or use Arrays.copyOf).
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Assignment, == and println(a) all act on the reference value: two aliases print the same address, while two equal-content arrays print different ones.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): b = a makes a second name for the same array (an alias); copying makes a second array: after a copy, changing b[i] leaves a[i] unchanged.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: aliasing lets two names work on one array without copying (as when an array is passed to a method), but in Chapter 1 code it is mostly a source of subtle bugs.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ArrayEqualityComparesValues: Conservation: replacing b = a with an element-copy loop keeps b's initial contents but breaks the link, so later changes to a no longer show in b. Reassigning a = new int[n] after b = a leaves b on the old array.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: assign an array variable when you want a second name for the same data. Use a copy loop or Arrays.copyOf for an independent copy, and an element loop or Arrays.equals to compare contents.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Assignment copies the reference, not the elements. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: b = a is used as a 'copy', and then b is modified while a is expected to stay unchanged (or the reverse)
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: == on arrays compares references, not contents. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: two separately created arrays with equal elements are compared with == (always false)
wrong: a == b is true when a and b hold the same values. | right: == compares whether the two arrays are the same array, not whether their values are equal.

wrong: An ArrayList is just an array, so it has a fixed length and is indexed with []. | right: An array has a fixed length and uses [] and .length; an ArrayList can grow and uses get, set and size().
wrong: assigning a reference copies the object | right: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong: a == b is true when a and b hold the same values. | right: == compares whether the two arrays are the same array, not whether their values are equal.
wrong: assigning a reference copies the object | right: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong: an ArrayList is an array (borderline; beyond Chapter 1 CS1) | right: An array has a fixed length and uses [] and .length; an ArrayList can grow and uses get, set and size().

wrong: b = a; for an array makes b a separate copy, so changing b[i] leaves a[i] unchanged. | right: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
Both follow from the array variable holding a reference (memory address): assignment and == act on that reference, and println(a) prints it.
b = a makes a second name for the same array (an alias); copying makes a second array: after a copy, changing b[i] leaves a[i] unchanged.
Because new creates one array and the variable stores only a reference to it, assigning that variable to another makes both names refer to the same array.
Because an array variable holds a reference, b = a copies the reference, so a and b name the same array.
